newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutor says Arizona governor lied to get loans.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutor says Arizona governor lied to get loans.

text.p: Arizona Gov. Fife Symington lied to borrow money for his ailing real-estate business, a prosecutor said Friday in statements opening the governor's trial on fraud, extortion and perjury charges.
"John Fife Symington is a smart and clever man who told lies to get millions of dollars in loans and then schemed to cover up those lies," Asst. U.S. Attorney David Schindler told jurors.
He also alleged Symington "abused his office as governor of the state of Arizona" in dealings with six union pension funds over a $10 million loan.
The defense portrayed the governor differently, saying Symington was "a man of vision" who may have made mistakes but who had no intent to defraud.
Defense attorney John Dowd blamed Symington's accountants for the mistakes in his financial statements and denied any attempt at extortion.
Symington, a 51-year-old Republican, faces 22 felony charges. Federal prosecutors will try to prove Symington committed fraud, extortion and perjury.
If convicted on even a single count, the two-term governor would be booted from the office he has held since 1991. He also faces a possible prison term.

In his opening statement in U.S. District Court, Schindler told the jury he would show Symington lied and schemed to save his ailing real-estate business and that there was a pattern of deceit in his business dealings.

The prosecutor said Symington submitted "blatantly false financial statements" to get loans from various institutions, including First Interstate Bank of Arizona, Valley National Bank, Mellon Bank, Dia-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd. and Citicorp Real Estate Inc.

Schindler cited examples of Symington's alleged lying by telling the jury that in 1990 he told one bank his net worth was $5.4 million, another that his worth was a negative $4.1 million and a third institution that he had not prepared a financial statement.
Symington also gave vastly differing values of his properties and of the percentage of his holding in them, Schindler said. He even lied about the value of his own home, he said.

Schindler said Symington was the beneficiary of "irrevocable spendthrift trusts" set up by his grandfather, but which he could not tap. Yet he told lending institutions he had access to the trust fund monies, Schindler said.

On the count of extortion, Schindler said Symington, who by then was governor, extorted an agreement from six union pension funds to release him from a personal loan guarantee he made to obtain a $10 million loan for a shopping center in Phoenix.
Schindler urged the jury to reach a verdict that would tell Symington "to stop lying and start playing by the same set of rules we all go by."
The defense, which made its opening argument later Friday, emphasized Symington's financial statements were only a part of the overall picture the lending institutions considered.
"The bankers loaned money to him on his reputation and performance as a developer," said Dowd, adding that Symington "just did the best he could from memory."

Dowd said it was Symington's accountants, Coopers & Lybrand, who should be blamed for the mistakes. "Some errors they caught, many they missed and they just dropped the ball. The accountants committed a "gross failure to serve and protect their client," he said.
Coopers & Lybrand reached a settlement with the government in September 1996, paying a penalty of $2.275 million to clear them of any charges in the case.
